findings.text: The page lives at Athena's address, but its title and almost all of its body are about a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets one sentence on Athena and then a long technical study of something they may never have heard of.

This opening sentence works: a newcomer can say what Athena is. It is the only description of Athena's own features, though, and the page never shows the request flow, the checking step or the cost records it mentions.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page explains why the study exists, and the claim links really do point to specific file lines at a pinned commit. That makes the case convincingly. What it does not say is why a newcomer would want a tool like this or when they would use it.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: The page links to the next steps from the top, and they give a concrete command to try. But they skip the clone step, say nothing about what you need first (a Rust toolchain? AI model access or keys?), and do not say what output to expect.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: The firstmate summary is clear. It explains backlog, worker and worktree in plain words before using them, so a reader can tell what firstmate does in one paragraph.

Most of the page is a dense state machine: transition ids, guards, exit codes, pending-close records and counters. That is useful to a firstmate contributor but hard going for a first-time visitor, and nothing tells newcomers they can skip it.
findings.source: Transitions cards, e.g. t2: "the spawn is deferred with exit 75 and the item stays queued ... lock contention or an unreadable capacity declaration refuses with exit 1"

findings.text: Some definitions in "Words used first" depend on terms that have no definition of their own, such as "merge authority", "guarded fast-forward" and "open captain call". A reader without git or firstmate background will get stuck on them.
findings.source: "local-only landing ... once the merge authority approves"

findings.text: The limits section is honest, but it uses Athena's internal wording ("job", "recorded boundary", "edge") that the page never explains. A stranger cannot tell what these limits mean.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate, so no failure or retry edge was observed"

findings.text: This section and the footer point to a repository folder the reader has not seen and get no link. To a newcomer they read as internal bookkeeping.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
